subject.name: ReactJS
subject.description: Prepare for React interviews, from fundamentals and component design to state, Hooks, forms, performance, routing, testing, accessibility, and modern React patterns.

topics.name: React Fundamentals
topics.description: React's declarative UI model, JSX, elements, and rendering.

topics.name: Components, Props & Composition
topics.description: Function components, props, children, and reusable component design.

topics.name: State & Event Handling
topics.description: Local state, immutable updates, event handlers, and state ownership.

topics.name: Rendering, Lists & Conditional UI
topics.description: Conditional rendering, list rendering, keys, and reconciliation.

topics.name: Hooks & Effects
topics.description: Rules of Hooks, useState, useEffect, useRef, memoization, and effect cleanup.

topics.name: Forms, Context & State Management
topics.description: Controlled forms, validation, Context API, reducers, and shared state.

topics.name: Performance, Routing & APIs
topics.description: Render optimization, code splitting, routing, API integration, and application structure.

topics.name: Testing, Accessibility & Modern React
topics.description: Component testing, accessible UI, error boundaries, portals, Suspense, and SSR concepts.

questions.question: How does a parent normally pass data to a child component?
questions.explanation: Props are inputs supplied by a parent and allow a child component to be configured.

questions.question: Should a child component mutate props it receives?

options.text: No; props should be treated as read-only
Yes, whenever the child needs a change
Only object props can be mutated

questions.explanation: A component should not mutate props. The owner should update state and pass the new value down.

questions.question: What does the special children prop represent?

options.text: Content nested between a component's opening and closing tags
All DOM nodes in the document

questions.explanation: Nested JSX is passed through props.children, enabling wrapper and layout components.

questions.question: Which is a valid function component declaration?
questions.explanation: A function component is a JavaScript function that returns React-renderable content. Component names start with an uppercase letter.

questions.question: Why do component names start with an uppercase letter in JSX?

options.text: JSX uses capitalization to distinguish custom components from built-in HTML tags

questions.explanation: A lowercase JSX tag such as div is treated as a built-in element; an uppercase identifier such as Profile refers to a component.

questions.question: What is component composition?

options.text: Building larger UI pieces by combining smaller components
Putting all code in one component
Using inheritance for every UI relationship

questions.explanation: Composition uses components as building blocks and often gives more flexibility than deep inheritance.

questions.question: What is a render prop?

options.text: A function passed as a prop so a component can delegate part of its rendering to the caller

questions.explanation: A render prop shares behavior while letting the consumer decide what UI to render. Hooks and composition are common alternatives today.

questions.question: When is children-based composition especially useful?

options.text: When a child must mutate its parent
For reusable layouts, panels, dialogs, and containers around caller-provided content

questions.explanation: A wrapper can provide shared layout or behavior while callers supply inner content through children.

questions.question: How can a reusable Button component support different visual styles?

options.text: Read the caller's local variables automatically
Create a separate React root per style
Accept a variant prop and map it to the appropriate classes or styles
Change the source code for each usage

questions.explanation: A variant prop creates a clear component API and allows the same component to support primary, secondary, and other styles.

questions.question: What is a compound component pattern?

options.text: Related components coordinate state and structure, often through context or controlled props
One component contains the entire application

questions.explanation: Compound components expose coordinated pieces such as Tabs, Tabs.List, and Tabs.Panel while keeping the API expressive.

questions.question: Which prop normally controls the current value of a React text input?
questions.explanation: A controlled text input receives its current value from state and updates it in onChange.

questions.question: Which event is commonly used to handle changes in a React text input?
questions.explanation: React's onChange event is used to respond to input changes and update the state controlling the field.

questions.question: How can a form's default browser submission be prevented?

options.text: Set the form key to null

questions.explanation: preventDefault prevents the browser's default navigation or submission behavior so the application can handle the submit event.

questions.question: What is an uncontrolled input?

options.text: An input that cannot be edited
An input that always submits automatically
An input whose current value is primarily managed by the DOM

questions.explanation: Uncontrolled inputs keep their current value in the DOM. A ref can read the value, and defaultValue can set its initial value.

questions.question: Which JSX attribute associates a label with a form control?
questions.explanation: JSX uses htmlFor to map to the HTML for attribute. Its value should match the control's id.

questions.question: What is a common issue when an input switches between uncontrolled and controlled modes?

options.text: The form stops receiving submit events
React may warn because the input changes between DOM-managed and state-managed modes
The browser changes the input type

questions.explanation: Keep a controlled input's value consistently defined, often using an empty string for an initially empty text input.

questions.question: How should a checkbox be controlled in React?

options.text: Use checked and update state in onChange
Set the DOM checked property during render

questions.explanation: Checkbox state is represented by checked. The handler reads event.target.checked.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of React Context?

options.text: Make a value available to components in a subtree without passing it through every intermediate component

questions.explanation: Context shares values such as theme, locale, or user information through a component tree and can reduce prop drilling.

questions.question: What does useReducer return?

options.text: A DOM reference and cleanup function
The current state and a dispatch function
A state value and numeric setter only

questions.explanation: useReducer returns state and dispatch. The reducer receives the current state and an action and returns the next state.

questions.question: Why is Context not automatically a complete replacement for every state-management library?

options.text: Context transports values but does not itself provide all features such as selectors, caching, or async workflows

questions.explanation: Context is a value propagation mechanism. Larger applications may need additional patterns for derived selectors, caching, complex updates, and asynchronous workflows.

questions.question: Why should API responses be treated as untrusted even when TypeScript interfaces describe them?

options.text: TypeScript types are erased at runtime and do not validate the actual network payload
The browser modifies every JSON response

questions.explanation: Static types do not inspect runtime data. Validate external payloads when correctness or security requires it.

questions.question: What is React primarily used for?
questions.explanation: React is a JavaScript library for building interactive user interfaces from reusable components.

questions.question: What is a React component?

options.text: A reusable piece of UI that can be composed with other components

questions.explanation: Components split a UI into reusable pieces. Function components commonly receive props and return React elements.

questions.question: What is JSX?

options.text: A replacement for the JavaScript runtime
A syntax extension that lets you describe UI with markup-like syntax in JavaScript

questions.explanation: JSX is transformed by build tooling into JavaScript calls that create React elements.

questions.question: How do you embed a JavaScript expression inside JSX?

options.text: Use angle brackets around the variable
Wrap the expression in curly braces

questions.explanation: Curly braces switch from JSX markup into a JavaScript expression, for example a user name or item count.

questions.question: What does declarative UI mean in React?

options.text: Describe what the UI should look like for the current state
Write HTML strings for every event

questions.explanation: React lets components describe the desired UI. React handles reconciling changes to the rendered output.

questions.question: What is React reconciliation?

options.text: The process of determining how to update the rendered UI from a new element tree

questions.explanation: Reconciliation compares previous and next React element descriptions to determine necessary host updates.

questions.question: Which change can cause a function component to render again?

options.text: Any function call anywhere in the app
A state update, changed props, or a changed context value it consumes

questions.explanation: Components may render due to their own state, parent renders with new props, or consumed context updates. Development checks can also cause extra renders.

questions.question: What is the difference between a React element and a component?

options.text: A component is a CSS class
An element describes what to render; a component is a function or class that can produce elements
An element is always a DOM node

questions.explanation: A component is reusable UI logic. JSX creates element descriptions that React uses during rendering.

questions.question: Why should rendering be kept free of side effects?

options.text: Rendering should be predictable and may be repeated, so side effects belong in event handlers or effects
React does not allow functions in render
Side effects only work in class components

questions.explanation: A render should calculate UI from current inputs. Starting requests or subscriptions during render can cause repeated or inconsistent side effects.

questions.question: What determines whether React preserves state for a component between renders?

options.text: Its position and identity in the rendered tree, including element type and key

questions.explanation: React associates state with component identity in the tree. Changing the type or key can cause the old subtree to be replaced and state reset.

questions.question: What are React Hooks?

options.text: Functions that let function components use React features such as state and context

questions.explanation: Hooks expose React capabilities to function components and custom Hooks.

questions.question: What is a core Rule of Hooks?

options.text: Call Hooks from ordinary utility functions
Call Hooks at the top level of React components or custom Hooks

questions.explanation: Hooks must be called in the same order on every render. Avoid conditions, loops, and nested callbacks.

questions.question: What does useRef return?

options.text: A promise for the next render
A new DOM node every call
A mutable object whose current property persists across renders
A setter that always causes rendering

questions.explanation: A ref object persists between renders, and changing current does not trigger a render. It is useful for DOM references and non-visual values.

questions.question: What is useEffect primarily used for?

options.text: Synchronizing a component with external systems

questions.explanation: Effects synchronize with systems such as subscriptions, timers, browser APIs, or network connections. Derived values usually do not require an effect.

questions.question: What does useMemo return?

options.text: A memoized result of a calculation while its dependencies remain unchanged
A callback guaranteed to run once

questions.explanation: useMemo caches a calculation result between renders. It is a performance optimization, not a correctness requirement.

questions.question: What does the dependency array of useEffect tell React?

options.text: Which reactive values the effect depends on

questions.explanation: When dependencies change, React runs cleanup for the previous effect and then runs the effect again.

questions.question: What is the cleanup function returned by an effect commonly used for?

options.text: Unsubscribing, clearing timers, aborting requests, or releasing resources

questions.explanation: Cleanup reverses or releases external synchronization established by the effect. It runs before a changed effect re-runs and on unmount.

questions.question: Why should Hooks not be called inside an if statement?

options.text: Conditional calls can change Hook call order between renders

questions.explanation: React associates Hook state with call order. Conditional calls can shift that order and associate state with the wrong Hook.

questions.question: What is a custom Hook?

options.text: A function starting with use that can call other Hooks to reuse stateful logic
A component that must render a button
A Hook that can only be called once

questions.explanation: Custom Hooks extract reusable stateful logic. Each call has independent Hook state unless it intentionally uses shared external state or context.

questions.question: Why should useMemo not be used to guarantee semantic persistence of a value?

options.text: It always returns a new value
It is a performance optimization and React may discard the cached value in some circumstances

questions.explanation: Code should remain correct if a memoized value is recalculated. Use state or a ref when a value must persist for semantic reasons.

questions.question: What does React.memo do?

options.text: It converts a component into a class
It can skip re-rendering when props compare equal

questions.explanation: React.memo memoizes a component based on props comparison. Its own state and consumed context can still cause renders.

questions.question: What is useCallback used for?

options.text: Storing a function in the DOM
Preventing a function from reading props
Memoizing a function reference while its dependencies remain unchanged

questions.explanation: useCallback returns a memoized function reference. It can help when referential stability matters to memoized children or dependencies.

questions.question: What is code splitting?

options.text: Splitting a component into DOM nodes
Breaking application code into smaller chunks that can be loaded when needed
Combining every file into one large bundle

questions.explanation: Code splitting reduces the initial JavaScript payload by loading parts of an application on demand.

questions.question: What does React.lazy help with?

options.text: Loading a component dynamically when it is rendered

questions.explanation: React.lazy loads a component through a dynamic import and is commonly paired with Suspense for a loading fallback.

questions.question: What is client-side routing?

options.text: Changing the displayed view based on the URL without a full document navigation for every route

questions.explanation: Client-side routers map URLs to UI views and manage browser history. The server must still serve the app entry point for supported routes.

questions.question: Why should an API request generally not start directly in the component body?

options.text: Requests can only be made from CSS
Rendering can run repeatedly, so the request could be started multiple times

questions.explanation: Keep render pure. Start synchronization in an effect, user-triggered requests in event handlers, or use a data-fetching framework.

questions.question: Why use TypeScript types for API response data?

options.text: They document expected data shapes and provide compile-time checking
They validate JSON at runtime automatically

questions.explanation: TypeScript helps catch incompatible property access at compile time, but types are erased at runtime and do not validate untrusted JSON.

questions.question: What is route-level code splitting used for?

options.text: Loading code for a route when needed to reduce the initial bundle

questions.explanation: Lazy-loading route components can reduce initial bundle size, especially in applications with many feature areas.

questions.question: Why can React.memo fail to skip a child render when data looks unchanged?

options.text: The child has a display name
The child has a CSS class
The parent may pass a newly created object or function prop on each render

questions.explanation: Shallow comparison sees new object and function references as changed. Stable references may help when profiling shows a real problem.

questions.question: Which JavaScript method is commonly used to render an array of items in JSX?
questions.explanation: map transforms each data item into a React element, commonly producing a repeated list.

questions.question: Why does React ask for a key when rendering a list?

options.text: To create a separate React root
To identify items across renders so React can track their identity

questions.explanation: Keys help React match items when inserted, removed, or reordered. Use stable identifiers from the data.

questions.question: What is usually the best key for database records rendered in a list?

options.text: The array index in every situation
A random number generated during render

questions.explanation: A stable ID preserves identity across reordering and insertion. Index keys can associate component state with the wrong record.

questions.question: How can JSX render one of two branches based on a condition?

options.text: Use if directly between JSX attributes
Use a ternary expression such as condition ? <A /> : <B />

questions.explanation: The ternary operator is a concise way to choose between JSX branches.

questions.question: What does a React Fragment provide?

options.text: A CSS class for all children
A way to group siblings without adding an extra DOM element

questions.explanation: Fragments allow multiple sibling elements without an unnecessary wrapper in the DOM.

questions.question: Why can an array index be a problematic key when items can be reordered?

options.text: React may associate component state with the wrong item after positions change

questions.explanation: Index keys identify positions rather than records. Reordering can cause component instances and input state to be reused for different records.

questions.question: What happens when a component's key changes between renders?

options.text: React treats it as a different identity and recreates the subtree, resetting local state
The key becomes a normal prop

questions.explanation: A changed key tells React that the previous and next elements are different identities, so the old subtree is replaced.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall with the expression count && <Badge />?

options.text: It prevents the component from mounting
If count is zero, React may render the numeric zero

questions.explanation: Logical AND returns the left operand when it is falsy. Since zero is renderable, use a boolean condition such as count > 0 && ... when appropriate.

questions.question: What does changing an element's type at the same tree position generally cause?

options.text: React replaces that subtree rather than preserving the previous component state

questions.explanation: Element type contributes to identity. A different type at the same position generally causes unmounting and mounting of a new subtree.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of stable keys in dynamic lists?

options.text: Preserve the intended identity of each item through insertions, removals, and reordering

questions.explanation: Stable keys let reconciliation match logical records rather than their current positions.

questions.question: Which Hook adds local state to a function component?
questions.explanation: useState returns the current state value and a setter that schedules an update.

questions.question: What does calling a useState setter do?

options.text: Schedules an update so React can render using the new state

questions.explanation: A setter requests an update. React may batch updates, so the state variable does not change immediately in the current render.

questions.question: How should an array in React state generally be updated?

options.text: Store it in a global variable
Create a new array using methods such as map, filter, or spread
Mutate the existing array with push

questions.explanation: Treat state immutably. A new array reference makes the update explicit and supports reliable change detection.

questions.question: How do you attach a click handler to a React button?

options.text: Use onClick and pass the handler function
Use click as a string attribute
Use lowercase onclick with a string

questions.explanation: React event props use camelCase. Pass a function reference such as onClick={handleClick} rather than invoking it during render.

questions.question: When is a functional state update useful?

options.text: When the next state depends on the previous state

questions.explanation: A setter such as setCount(previous => previous + 1) uses the latest queued state value.

questions.question: Why might three calls to setCount(count + 1) in one handler not increment by three?

options.text: React ignores all but the last setter
Each expression can read the same count snapshot from the current render

questions.explanation: Use functional updates such as setCount(c => c + 1) so each queued update builds on the previous value.

questions.question: What does lifting state up mean?

options.text: Copying state independently into every child
Persisting every value in the URL
Moving shared state to the closest common ancestor of components that need it

questions.explanation: A common owner creates a single source of truth and coordinates children through props and callbacks.

questions.question: What is a controlled input?

options.text: An input stored only in cookies
An input whose value is driven by React state and updated through an event handler
An input that cannot be edited
An input controlled only by CSS

questions.explanation: A controlled input receives value from state and updates that state in onChange.

questions.question: Why pass a callback from a parent to a child?

options.text: So the child can notify the parent about an event or user action
So the child can mutate parent props

questions.explanation: Callback props provide a communication path from child to parent, allowing the parent to update its own state.

questions.question: What is state colocation?

options.text: Moving all state into one global object
Keeping state close to the components that use it

questions.explanation: Colocation clarifies ownership and limits unnecessary sharing. Lift state only when multiple components need to coordinate.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a unit test for a React component?

options.text: Verify component behavior for given inputs and user interactions

questions.explanation: Component tests verify observable behavior such as rendered content, interactions, and state changes.

questions.question: Why are accessible names important for buttons and form controls?

options.text: They help assistive technologies identify the purpose of controls

questions.explanation: Accessible names allow screen-reader users and other assistive technologies to understand a control's purpose.

questions.question: Which HTML element is generally preferable for an action that performs an operation?
questions.explanation: A semantic button provides built-in keyboard behavior, focusability, and accessibility semantics.

questions.question: What is an error boundary used for?

options.text: Catch rendering errors in descendant components and display fallback UI

questions.explanation: Error boundaries catch errors during descendant rendering and certain lifecycle paths. They do not catch every event-handler or asynchronous error.

questions.question: What is a common benefit of testing user-visible behavior?

options.text: Tests are less coupled to internal structure and better reflect user interactions

questions.explanation: Tests based on roles, labels, text, and interactions are often more resilient than tests of private implementation details.

questions.question: What are React Testing Library userEvent utilities designed for?

options.text: Simulating user interactions in a way that is closer to real browser usage

questions.explanation: userEvent simulates higher-level interactions such as typing and clicking, allowing tests to assert visible outcomes.

questions.question: Why should asynchronous UI updates often be awaited in component tests?

options.text: The update may happen after a promise, event, or scheduled render completes

questions.explanation: Use asynchronous queries or wait utilities to avoid asserting before the UI has updated.

questions.question: What does createPortal allow a component to do?

options.text: Render children into a different DOM node while keeping them in the React tree

questions.explanation: Portals are useful for modals and tooltips that need different DOM placement. Events still propagate according to the React tree.

questions.question: What is hydration in a server-rendered React application?

options.text: Attaching React behavior to HTML that was already rendered on the server

questions.explanation: Hydration lets React take over server-generated markup and attach event handling. Initial client output must be compatible with server output.

questions.question: What is a purpose of useTransition in modern React?

options.text: Guarantee a network request finishes in the background
Mark updates as non-urgent so React can keep the interface responsive

questions.explanation: useTransition marks certain state updates as transitions so React can prioritize urgent updates such as typing over non-urgent rendering work.
